name: Water cutting / dehydration

card.summary: Deliberate fluid loss to look leaner or make weight; documented in combat sports, with dehydration-related deaths and regulator responses.
card.aka: Water cut, weight cutting, dehydration cut, sweatsuit cutting
card.note: Associated with documented deaths in combat sports; dehydration can cause serious complications.

quick.overview:
Water cutting is the deliberate reduction of body water, often through sweating, saunas, sweatsuits or fluid manipulation, to lose weight quickly or look drier and leaner. It is best documented in combat sports, where athletes cut to a lower weight class before weigh-ins, and it is also referred to in bodybuilding contexts for a 'dry' look.

Sports medicine commentary cited here describes it as dangerous, and several athletes have died while cutting weight. Some organizations have changed their rules in response.
quick.mechanism: Methods described include restricting food and fluids, water-loading, exercise-induced sweating, sweatsuits and saunas. Because sweat is mostly water, weight lost this way is largely fluid, which returns with rehydration.
quick.risks: Dehydration can cause headache, fatigue, confusion, seizures, heatstroke, hypernatremia and kidney problems. Losses of 15 to 25 percent of body water are described as fatal. Deaths in weight-cutting athletes in 2015, 2016 and 2017 have been reported.

lead: Water cutting, also called a dehydration cut or water manipulation, is the practice of deliberately reducing body water to look leaner or lighter. Physique competitors use it in the last stage before a show to sharpen muscle definition and vascularity, combat-sport athletes use it to reach a lower weight class, and some people in looksmaxxing and fitness circles use sweating, fluid restriction or sauna sessions to look drier, with a tighter face and clearer jawline.[1][3]

Methods described include restricting food and fluids, water-loading beforehand, and sweating through exercise, sweat suits or saunas.[1] A general description of bodybuilding notes that competitors combine carbohydrate loading and dehydration in the final stage to achieve maximum muscle definition and vascularity.[3] The idea is that water held under the skin softens the outline of muscle and facial structure, so reducing it makes edges and veins look sharper for a short period.

Medical references describe dehydration as a deficit of total body water. Mild losses are associated with thirst, headache and impaired concentration, and severe or rapid losses with serious complications.[2][5] Several combat-sport deaths during weight cutting between 2015 and 2017 led organisations to change their rules.[1] Some bodybuilders describe the visual result of a water cut as smaller than expected.[10]

chain: Body water is reduced over hours or days
Less fluid sits under the skin and around muscle
Sharper muscle definition and a drier-looking face for a short time
angle.text: Practitioners cut water to show more definition and vascularity on stage, or to appear leaner in photographs. The change is temporary because fluids are replaced afterwards.[3]

paras: Weight cutting is described as having two forms: losing fat and muscle over weeks before an event, and losing water in the final days.[1] Some athletes diet and add aerobic exercise instead, aiming to improve their strength-to-mass ratio.[1] The practice is used in combat sports, rowing and equestrian sports, where a lower weight is an advantage.[1]

In physique sports, the final-stage routine is described as pairing carbohydrate loading with dehydration for definition and vascularity.[3] Competitors typically also tan and shave before going on stage.[3]

The look sought is a drier, tighter appearance: visible muscle separation, vascularity and, in the face, more defined cheekbones and jaw. Reports from practitioners vary. One T Nation member posted before-and-after pictures from a water cut with a difference of about 15 lb in water weight and described very little visible change.[10]
Dehydration itself is described as producing sunken eyes and dry mucous membranes among its signs.[2]

A comprehensive review of dehydration physiology distinguishes between loss of water from inside cells and iso-osmotic loss from the extracellular space, and discusses assessment by osmolality and volume.[6] A consensus statement from a multidisciplinary group defines dehydration and reviews diagnostic methods and clinical implications.[9]

Dehydration signs include thirst, headache, nausea, reduced urine, confusion and in severe cases seizures. Acute complications include hypovolemic shock, coma, heatstroke and hypernatremia, and rehydrating too quickly risks cerebral oedema.[2]

Reported deaths while cutting weight include Yang Jian Bing in December 2015, Jordan Coe in March 2016 and Jessica Lindsay in November 2017.[1] ONE Championship subsequently banned dehydration-based cutting and moved to a 'walking weight' model with urine specific gravity hydration testing.[1] A Perth physician urged hydration tests before bouts and warned in 2018 that deaths were inevitable without regulation.[1] In 2022 a regulator suspended a fighter for six months and fined him after he posted a video of himself vomiting while cutting.[1]

No studies found of deliberate water cutting for physique appearance. Research on dehydration more broadly includes a 2018 meta-analysis of 33 studies finding that dehydration impairs cognitive performance,[5] a review of cognition and mild dehydration describing impaired attention and memory at about 2 percent loss,[4] and randomised trials of mild dehydration and mood in young men and women.[7][8]

timeline.event: Chinese MMA fighter Yang Jian Bing dies while cutting weight; ONE Championship later bans dehydration-based cutting.[1]
Scottish Muay Thai fighter Jordan Coe dies while cutting weight in Thailand.[1]
Australian fighter Jessica Lindsay dies after extreme weight cutting.[1]
A Perth physician warns deaths will continue without hydration testing.[1]
A US regulator suspends a Bellator fighter for six months over a weight-cut video.[1]

lore.intro: Water cutting comes up in bodybuilding and strength forums as part of peak-week routines and as a way to appear leaner on camera. Accounts vary widely in how much visual change they report.[10]

claims.claim: Cutting water makes muscle and the face look sharper
claims.believers: Competitors say a short-term water reduction before a show brings out definition and vascularity.[3]
claims.experts: A general description of bodybuilding notes that competitors combine carbohydrate loading and dehydration for definition and vascularity.[3] No study has measured the visual effect.

claims.claim: A large water cut barely changes the look
claims.believers: One T Nation member posted comparison photos with roughly 15 lb of water difference and little visual change.[10]
claims.experts: No published studies have compared appearance before and after deliberate water cuts.

claims.claim: Sauna and sweatsuit sessions are a safe way to drop weight fast
claims.believers: Athletes report using them routinely to make weight.[1]
claims.experts: Clinicians and a regulator-backed physician describe acute water loss as very dangerous, and several deaths have been reported in combat sports.[1][2]
